lesson.title: hätte & wäre: The Subjunctive Twins
lesson.subtitle: hätte is had's subjunctive, wäre is were — the would-world of wishes and kind speech

hook.title: The Room English Locked
hook.content: English keeps exactly one fossil of its old subjunctive room: If I WERE you. That were — not was — is the sound of a world that isn't real: wishes, hypotheses, polite dreaming. German kept the whole room furnished. wäre is were's twin, same root (the *wes- of war/was), same would-world job. And hätte is had doing a second shift: the past form of haben, re-lit as 'would have' — Wenn ich Zeit hätte (if I had time), Ich hätte Lust (I would like). German builds its gentlest, most polite sentences out of past-tense shapes: the past is where hypotheticals live.

footnotes.title: The -e Is the Signal
footnotes.content: Compare the pairs: hatte (I had — real past) vs hätte (I would have — the would-world). war (I was) vs wäre (I would be). One letter, one whole reality: the umlauted -e marks the sentence as a hypothesis, a wish, or a politeness. Old English had the same pair — hæfde did duty for both — and German kept the distinction crisp.

pattern.title: The Would-World Conjugations
pattern.content: hätte: ich hätte, du hättest, er hätte, wir hätten ↔ I had, thou hadst (in its 'would' shift). wäre: ich wäre, du wärst, er wäre, wir wären ↔ I were, thou wert (the true English subjunctive!). The two great frames: WISHES — Wenn ich Geld hätte! (if only I had money), Wenn ich reich wäre! (if I were rich). SOFT STATEMENTS — Das wäre gut (that would be good), Ich wäre froh (I would be glad), Das wäre alles (that would be all — the politest way to finish an order). Notice wäre ↔ wert: English's thou wert WAS a subjunctive — the fossil in your own mouth.
pattern.linguist_note: Konjunktiv II from the preterite: Germanic built its hypothetical mood out of past forms (past = far from reality, mentally as well as temporally). That is why hätte looks exactly like hatte with dots — it IS the past form, repurposed by distance.

exercises.prompt: The would-world — match each soft form with its reading:
exercises.target_answer: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, Wenn ich reich wäre, Das wäre gut, Das wäre alles, Wenn ich Geld hätte, Ich wäre müde
exercises.explanation: Wishes take Wenn + hätte/wäre; soft statements use wäre alone. The -e marks the world as hypothetical. And the would-world is where families and names live: die Familie wünscht sich Zeit, and every new name arrives spelled out, one Buchstabe at a time.

exercises.prompt: Wish or memory? 'Wenn ich Zeit _____!' (if only I HAD time — a wish):
exercises.meaning: Wenn ich Zeit hätte = if I had time (would-world)
exercises.explanation: hatte is the plain past (I had — real); hätte is the would-world (I would have — hypothetical). One letter, one reality.

exercises.meaning: Wenn ich reich wäre = if I were rich
exercises.explanation: wäre ↔ were — the exact twin of English's one surviving subjunctive: if I WERE you.

exercises.prompt: Which English fossil verb-form is the true twin of 'wäre'?
exercises.explanation: Both are the *wes- root in its subjunctive shift. English kept one phrase; German kept the whole conjugation.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the wish, both verbs: 'If I had time, I would be glad'
exercises.target_answer: Wenn ich Zeit hätte wäre ich froh
exercises.meaning: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, wäre ich froh = if I had time, I would be glad
exercises.explanation: Two would-world verbs in one breath: hätte closes the Wenn-clause (verb-final!), wäre carries the main clause.

summary.outcome: Use hätte and wäre for wishes and soft statements, and distinguish them from hatte and war.

use_example.german: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, wäre ich froh.
use_example.english: If I had time, I would be glad.

summary.takeaway: hätte ↔ had, wäre ↔ were: the would-world wears past-tense clothes — and the -e is the signal.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: könnte, würde & the politeness escalator — could's old job, would's machine, and four ways to order a coffee.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from hätte & wäre: The Subjunctive Twins (Wenn ich Zeit hätte, wäre ich froh = if I had time, I would be glad):
twist.target_answer: Wenn ich Zeit hätte wäre ich froh
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wenn ich Zeit hätte wäre ich froh" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of hätte & wäre: The Subjunctive Twins without relying on short-term echo.

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

geld.context_translation: I have no money with me.
geld.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *geldą 'reward, payment' — kin to English geld and yield, NOT to gold. [wiktionary]

froh.context_phrase: Ich bin froh, dass du kommst.
froh.context_translation: I am glad that you are coming.
froh.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawaz 'quick, glad' — English frolic (via Dutch) is the named cognate. [wiktionary]

müde.context_phrase: Ich bin müde und gehe ins Bett.
müde.context_translation: I am tired and go to bed.
müde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *mōþī; only Dutch moe named — no English cognate, memorize this one. [wiktionary]

buchstabe.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *bōkstabô, literally book-stave: each letter was a stave carved for writing, first on beechwood; the page compares English bookstaff and bookstave. [wiktionary]

familie.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin familia — the same Latin source as English family. [wiktionary]

salat.etymology_derivation: 15th-century borrowing from Italian salata — the same Romance source as English salad. [wiktionary]

hähnchen.context_phrase: Wir essen Hähnchen mit Reis und Salat.
hähnchen.context_translation: We are eating chicken with rice and salad.
hähnchen.etymology_derivation: Hähnchen — diminutive of Hahn (rooster) with the -chen suffix; Hahn is the old Germanic cock-word, the same family as English hen (PIE *keh₂n-). [wiktionary]

schale.context_phrase: Die Banane hat eine gelbe Schale.
schale.context_translation: The banana has a yellow peel.
schale.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic skalo, meaning husk or shell; English shell and shale are cognates from the same Germanic root. [wiktionary]

lecken.etymology_derivation: From Old High German lecchōn, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną. English lick is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

krankenschwester.etymology_derivation: Kranker (ill one) + Schwester (sister) - a sick sister; Schwester is the exact twin of English sister (PIE *swésōr). [wiktionary]

kreuzung.etymology_derivation: kreuzen + -ung, from Kreuz, borrowed from Latin crux, crucis — the same Latin word that gave English cross, which English took via Old Irish and Old Norse. [wiktionary][etymonline]
